items.title: Former Porn Star Reveals Key to Unlocking Shame, Embracing Freedom
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "Shame is not God's intention for your life."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

If anyone knows the grip of shame, it’s a former porn star.

Joshua Broome spent years in the pornography industry before finding faith in God, abandoning a life driven by sexual sin and drug abuse, and becoming a husband and father to four boys.

Since his salvation 11 years ago, Broome has become an outspoken evangelist and advocate against the dangers of pornography. One of the barriers to healing, he explained to CBN News, is shame.

“Shame is not God’s intention for your life,” he said. “The solution to shame is connection, is confession.”

Before he learned the Gospel, Broome said it was shame — rather than enjoyment— that kept him trapped in the pornography industry for years. He explained that, while guilt reveals, “I’ve done something wrong,” shame wrongly convinces a person, “I am someone wrong.”

“If I believe that my only value is indicative of me selling myself for sex, well, then, of course I’m going to continue doing what I’ve done, because it’s just an overflow of who I am,” he said.

From the Old to the New Testament, the Bible is clear about the need for confession for spiritual healing.

In Proverbs 28:13, King Solomon wrote, “People who conceal their sins will not prosper, but if they confess and turn from them, they will receive mercy” (NLT).

Then, in 1 John 1:8-9, it’s written, “If we claim we have no sin, we are only fooling ourselves and not living in the truth. But if we confess our sins to him, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleans us from all wickedness” (NLT).

And in James 5:16, James wrote, “Confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The earnest prayer of a righteous person has great power and produces wonderful results” (NLT).

The key to breaking the cycle of shame, Broome emphasized, is honest and complete confession.

“The depth of your confession is going to equate to the level of your healing,” he said. “So say all of it.”

He continued, “The way that you own your past is you have to own it, and the way that you own it is you say it out loud because we can only be as free as we’re willing to be honest.”

For many, Broome said, the root of pornography use is not lust or even sex; more often than not, it’s tied to something much deeper: insecurity, loneliness, an unhealthy understanding of intimacy.

The truth is conversations about past sins or sin struggles are not easy. Broome and his wife, Hope, have had their fair share of difficult conversations over his sexual history. But the truth is, while accountability and responsibility are essential to spiritual growth, confession should be met with compassion.

“[My wife] looked at me and said, ‘Hey, I don’t want to minimize your pain … but I do want to tell you that you’re not defined by the worst thing you’ve ever done, and you won’t be defined by the greatest thing you ever do, because you’re not the author of you — God is,'” Broome recalled. “At the cross, the worst of us meets the best of God, and He wins. That’s how you defeat shame.”

Broome and his wife are the hosts of a new six-part series from XO Marriage, “Made Whole: Healing, Wholeness, and Holiness in a Sex-Saturated World.” You can access the course for free here.

Watch our wide-ranging conversation with Broome in the video above.

items.title: Celebrity Wishes for Perez Hilton’s Recovery — Then Takes It Back: Why?
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Perez Hilton’s livestream was the stuff of nightmares — a potentially demonic episode — and has laid bare the dark underbelly of social media, in more ways than one.

On the periphery of the scandal, a TikTok live video feed that ran nearly half an hour and showed Hilton covered in blood and repeatedly harming himself, was another troubling indication of cultural decay: a society that cares not about praying for our enemies but about getting even.

Jared Padalecki, who rose to fame in the early 2000s as one of the stars of “Gilmore Girls,” has used his clout to advocate for mental wellness, so it’s particularly striking to see him not only rescind but apologize for wishing Hilton well amidst his recovery from what was and will be a decisively defining and deeply dark moment in his life.

Initially, Padalecki wrote on social media, “I hope you are trying as best as you can to be kind to yourself right now. Please surround yourself with the love and support that all humans deserve.”

It wasn’t long before the “Supernatural” star faced swift condemnation for his kindhearted message to the celebrity gossip blogger. Padalecki deleted the post and apologized for publicly hoping for healing for Hilton, telling critics he “didn’t know” about the columnist’s career.

Padalecki went on to apologize for his “words caus[ing] any harm” and added he hopes everyone is “taking care of yourselves.”

It was Padalecki’s first instinct — his wish for Hilton’s healing — that was correct, regardless of Hilton’s checkered past and his indefensible work as a gossip blogger, actions that undoubtedly caused harm to the celebrities who were subject to his coverage.

That’s exactly what Jesus commands of us as His followers in Matthew 5:44-47 (NLT).

“But I say to you,” Jesus preached, “love your enemies! Pray for those who persecute you! In that way, you will be acting as true children of your Father in heaven.”

He went on to say, “For He gives His sunlight to both the evil and the good, and He sends rain on the just and the unjust alike. If you love only those who love you, what reward is there for that? Even corrupt tax collectors do that much. If you are kind only to your friends, how are you different from anyone else? Even pagans do that.”

Then, in Romans 12:17-21 (NLT), the Apostle Paul warned against taking revenge or seeking vengeance against others:

Never pay back evil with more evil. Do things in such a way that everyone can see you are honorable. Do all that you can to live in peace with everyone. Dear friends, never take revenge. Leave that to the righteous anger of God. For the Scriptures say, ‘I will take revenge; I will pay them back,’ says the Lord.

Instead, ‘If your enemies are hungry, feed them. If they are thirsty, give them something to drink. In doing this, you will heap burning coals of shame on their heads.’

Don’t let evil conquer you, but conquer evil by doing good.

Our petition for God to intervene for the healing of another human being made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27) should never be predicated on what he or she has done in the past. Rather, it should be evidence of an outpouring of gratitude for a forgiveness gifted to us by a Savior who asks each of us to forgive one another in the same way God, through Jesus, has forgiven us (Ephesians 4:32).

Hilton, who in recent months has professed a faith in Jesus, needs prayer — regardless of the sins of his past.

All of us should absolutely be held accountable for our errors, missteps, and wrongdoings; taking responsibility for our actions is a necessary consequence of the choices we each make in this life. None of that, though, absolves us of the duty to pray for those around us or to need the prayers of others.

In the King James Version translation of 1 Peter 2:9, the Apostle Peter wrote that believers are “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a peculiar people” in the world.

While social media is preying on our worst instincts — our fallen nature — to belittle, disparage, and denigrate, we follow a God who is calling us to do the opposite, to be peculiar by praying for the redemption of those trapped in dark places distant from the Lord.

As the psalmist wrote, I pray that, even as Hilton walks through the “darkest valley,” he would find the Shepherd who “leads me beside peaceful streams,” “renews my strength,” and “guides me along right paths” (Psalm 23:1-4, NLT).

items.title: One Worthy of Worship
items.author: Elisa Morgan
items.summary: One April afternoon, millions gathered along a mapped arc across Mexico and the United States to witness a rare total solar eclipse. Schools released children, small towns blossomed to receive travelers, neighbors set up lawn chairs in driveways donning protective glasses to take in the wonder. As t
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

One April afternoon, millions gathered along a mapped arc across Mexico and the United States to witness a rare total solar eclipse. Schools released children, small towns blossomed to receive travelers, neighbors set up lawn chairs in driveways donning protective glasses to take in the wonder. As television crews documented the countdown to “totality,” the crowd grew silent except for one repeated phrase: “Oh my God!”

That struck me. I don’t know for certain why those observers chose that phrase in that moment, but I suspect that as mortals encountered the rare and the astonishing, they seemed to need Someone to acknowledge. Someone to thank. Someone to worship. When we look heavenward, our response is awe. As David wrote, “The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of his hands” (Psalm 19:1).

Luke, the historian, reports Jesus’ last minutes on the cross. “It was about noon, and darkness came over the whole land until three in the afternoon, for the sun stopped shining” (23:44-45). Matthew shares a response to this revelation. “When the centurion and those with him who were guarding Jesus saw the earthquake and all that had happened, they were terrified, and exclaimed, ‘Surely he was the Son of God!’ ” (Matthew 27:54). They couldn’t help but acknowledge God as the Someone worthy of worship.

In humble awe, I worship You—my God.

items.title: Jesus’ Witness
items.author: John Blase
items.summary:
I’ve heard it said, “We can’t make our children believe. We can only give our children reason to believe what we believe.” That’s a wise observation—but how do we do it?
Of all people to take parenting advice from, the apostle Paul is seldom the first choice. It&r
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

I’ve heard it said, “We can’t make our children believe. We can only give our children reason to believe what we believe.” That’s a wise observation—but how do we do it?

Of all people to take parenting advice from, the apostle Paul is seldom the first choice. It’s likely that he had no children. Parents prefer to hear from someone who’s been-there-done-that, someone who knows about sleepless infants, the storms of puberty, and how it feels to pray for a prodigal. Yet Paul has something to teach us here.

Paul had been on his way to persecute Christians when Christ intervened. Paul fell to the ground, blinded (Acts 9:1-9). Soon he was visited by Ananias who restored his sight and explained his mission: “The God of our ancestors has chosen you to know his will and to see the Righteous One and to hear words from his mouth. You will be his witness to all people of what you have seen and heard” (22:14-15). Paul did witness, and God gave him a quiver-full of spiritual offspring. His “parenting approach” was to share what he’d seen, and to pray.

Whether parenting our own children or interacting with others, we can’t make them believe. Rather, we witness with our words and lives as to what we’ve seen and heard. And we pray. Our God, who sent Paul to the gentiles, sends us with the same instruction: witness so they may believe. Then entrust them to our Father who loves them.

items.title: Two Guys Are Putting Fake Tech Ads All Over NYC Subways, and They’re Pretty Incredible
items.author: RELEVANT
items.summary: New York’s subways have become so saturated with ads for AI startups that comedians Harris Alterman and Dave Ross decided to invent a few of their own. They created 10 completely fake tech companies, designed professional-looking subway ads for them and temporarily hung full-size vinyl banners insid
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

New York’s subways have become so saturated with ads for AI startups that comedians Harris Alterman and Dave Ross decided to invent a few of their own.

They created 10 completely fake tech companies, designed professional-looking subway ads for them and temporarily hung full-size vinyl banners inside two Brooklyn stations. The products don’t exist. Neither do the companies. But the ads look convincing because Alterman and Ross copied the vague, jargon-heavy language that has become nearly impossible to avoid in tech advertising.

It took them about 30 minutes to write all 10.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Harris Alterman (@theharrisalterman)

One fake company, Zordle, promises to “orchestrate agentic workflows at scale.” Another poses the disruptive question Silicon Valley apparently wasn’t brave enough to tackle: “What if forks were spoons?”

There’s Strawberr.ai, which offers “Business intelligence. Reinvented.” Another promises to “unlock the intelligence layer of your organization.” The names change. The language barely does.

Alterman has a term for it: “slop voice.”

“The ads kind of have to be vague, because the product is vague,” he said.

After printing the ads at the same scale as actual subway advertisements, Alterman and Ross installed them, filmed the stunt and took them down immediately. Their video has since pulled in more than 5 million views and 250,000 likes.

The joke landed because the fake ads don’t look especially fake. Someone walking through the station could reasonably assume there really was a venture-backed company somewhere trying to revolutionize spoons.

And New Yorkers have been getting plenty of opportunities to study the source material. Tech companies accounted for 15% of subway and bus advertising in New York during the first quarter of 2026, according to Outfront Media data reported by Semafor, up 50% from a year earlier.

But Alterman thinks the response goes beyond people enjoying a good AI joke.

“I feel like it does connect you to other people to be like, look, we’re all going crazy,” he said.

That might be the real reason millions of people immediately got it. AI advertising has developed its own strange dialect, full of companies promising to transform work with products described in language that somehow becomes less comprehensible the longer it goes on.

Alterman and Ross barely had to exaggerate it. They just removed the last little bit of meaning.

The project has since expanded beyond the subway. At a recent pop-up featuring the fake ads, Alterman said a Palantir employee showed up wearing a Palantir hat and told him people inside the company had been talking about the project.

Then the employee offered an unsolicited clarification: “I don’t work on the evil stuff at Palantir. I do something else.”

At some point, the parody just writes itself.

items.title: Friday, August 14, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus teaches the sacred unity of marriage.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Ezekiel 16:1-15, 60, 63

 The word of the Lord came to me: Mortal, make known to Jerusalem her abominations, and say, Thus says the Lord God to Jerusalem: Your origin and your birth were in the land of the Canaanites; your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite. As for your birth, on the day you were born your navel cord was not cut, nor were you washed with water to cleanse you, nor rubbed with salt, nor wrapped in cloths. No eye pitied you, to do any of these things for you out of compassion for you; but you were thrown out in the open field, for you were abhorred on the day you were born.

I passed by you, and saw you flailing about in your blood. As you lay in your blood, I said to you, “Live! and grow up like a plant of the field.” You grew up and became tall and arrived at full womanhood; your breasts were formed, and your hair had grown; yet you were naked and bare.

I passed by you again and looked on you; you were at the age for love. I spread the edge of my cloak over you, and covered your nakedness: I pledged myself to you and entered into a covenant with you, says the Lord God, and you became mine. Then I bathed you with water and washed off the blood from you, and anointed you with oil. I clothed you with embroidered cloth and with sandals of fine leather; I bound you in fine linen and covered you with rich fabric. I adorned you with ornaments: I put bracelets on your arms, a chain on your neck, a ring on your nose, earrings in your ears, and a beautiful crown upon your head. You were adorned with gold and silver, while your clothing was of fine linen, rich fabric, and embroidered cloth. You had choice flour and honey and oil for food. You grew exceedingly beautiful, fit to be a queen. Your fame spread among the nations on account of your beauty, for it was perfect because of my splendor that I had bestowed on you, says the Lord God.

But you trusted in your beauty, and played the whore because of your fame, and lavished your whorings on any passer-by.

Yet I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish with you an everlasting covenant.

In order that you may remember and be confounded, and never open your mouth again because of your shame, when I forgive you all that you have done, says the Lord God.

Psalm
Isaiah 12:2-3, 4bcd, 5-6

Surely God is my salvation;
    I will trust, and will not be afraid,
for the Lord God is my strength and my might;
    he has become my salvation.
With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation. And you will say in that day:
Give thanks to the Lord,
    call on his name;
make known his deeds among the nations;
    proclaim that his name is exalted.
Sing praises to the Lord, for he has done gloriously;
    let this be known in all the earth.
Shout aloud and sing for joy, O royal Zion,
    for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 19:3-12

Some Pharisees came to him, and to test him they asked, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause?” He answered, “Have you not read that the one who made them at the beginning ‘made them male and female,’ and said, ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh’? So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.” They said to him, “Why then did Moses command us to give a certificate of dismissal and to divorce her?” He said to them, “It was because you were so hard-hearted that Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. And I say to you, whoever divorces his wife, except for unchastity, and marries another commits adultery.”

His disciples said to him, “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry.” But he said to them, “Not everyone can accept this teaching, but only those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth, and there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by others, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let anyone accept this who can.”

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus teaches the sacred unity of marriage. The physical, sexual, psychological, economic, and loving bonds between a man and a woman have, ultimately, a sacred purpose: to act as a conduit of the divine life in the world.

How does this work? In the unity of a man and a woman, which becomes in so many ways fruitful, we see an image of the Blessed Trinity: The Father and the Son love one another to such a perfect degree that their love gives birth to the Holy Spirit.

A married couple should see their relationship as an icon of the Holy Trinity—and more to it, a means by which the Trinitarian love bursts forth into the world. The two partners have a mission before God.

St. Paul saw that Christian marriage had a precisely Christian purpose: to symbolize the love of Christ and the Church. As a husband loves his wife (and as she loves him), so does Christ love the Church and the Church (at least ideally) love him. What does Christ’s love for his Church look like? Well, it’s a deeply joyful reality, for it is the sharing of the divine life.

items.title: ‘Unsung Hero’ and Rudyard Kipling’s Ifs for Men
items.author: Barnabas Ney
items.summary:
Barnabas Ney

It is by bringing our sins and weaknesses to the light that we allow our pride to be taken away and replaced by the peace of surrender.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Barnabas Ney

In his famous poem “If,” Rudyard Kipling’s narrator says to his son that if he can achieve certain things, then he would be a man. If he can keep his head, if he can trust himself, if he can behave a certain way, then manhood and success would surely be his. While this poem reveals a certain undeniable wisdom, it also naturally gives rise to the thorny question that many of us men ask ourselves from time to time: What if I can’t? What if I can’t trust myself? What if I can’t bear to “lose, and start again at [my] beginning?” (line 19). Am I then not a man?

These questions find a beautiful expression in the 2024 film Unsung Hero. This movie is one that I now widely recommend to my male friends who are considering marriage or are newly married. This true story follows the Smallbone family as they leave Australia after a ruinous financial decision by the father, David. Although the titular character and the real unsung hero of the story is the wife and mother, Helen, it is a poignant depiction of the anxiety that faces men who do not know if they can be a good man, husband, or father. The film is also filled with stirring music written by the band For King + Country.

Pursuing an employment opportunity, David and Helen move with their seven children to America. Ultimately disappointed in his job, David must face challenges that will resonate with many men in today’s milieu. Unemployment, the disappointment of children, the death of a father, and a sense of unworthiness are just a few of these challenges. In the midst of all this, perhaps the most difficult battle David faces is against his own pride. This is not the hubris of success and recognition but the grasping and painful rebellion against the slow realization that he is unable to provide for and protect his family as he feels he ought to. David is not able to solve these challenges by himself. Instead, he becomes necessarily dependent in various ways on the generosity of his neighbors and on God. His pride rebels. 

Throughout the film, David’s father seeks to encourage him by their tradition of quoting bits of Kipling’s poem “If.” Though separated by half a world, his father seeks to motivate and remind David to “dream—and not make dreams your master” and to “wait and not be tired by waiting.” Yet as the disappointments compile and David reaches the limits of his endurance, in his frustration and anxiety he eventually refuses to accept his father’s encouragement. Tragically, his father dies soon after and David is unable even to fly home for the funeral. David seems to be constantly stuck on the wrong side of every if.

In a series of sequences that are built throughout the film, we are given insight into three valuable lessons. 

1. There may come times in a man’s life when the ifs of life seem completely overwhelming.

Recent psychological research is showing that uncertainty can be a significant contributing factor to negative mental health. This seems to hold particularly true of youth and men. In Unsung Hero, we see that ifs are not only uncertainty about future outcomes but the terrible question of what does it mean if I fail? Since so many men are told that success and self-mastery are the proofs of manhood, it is unsurprising that failure and weakness can become almost existential crises for men. We should not be surprised when men come to face moments of uncertainty in themselves and their abilities. 

What this movie depicts so beautifully is that when we do experience failure and loss, there can be a path forward even if we do not initially respond as we ought. We do not lose all hope of grace, good, and God. In the movie, David initially overcomes a very significant career and financial setback, yet when his stoic response does not lead to “the Earth and all that is in it” (line 31), he becomes frustrated, angry, and self-pitying. It is here that the real crisis occurs.

2. Pride is just as insidious an enemy when we seem to have nothing left.

At the height of his loss and frustrations, David is confronted in a climactic argument by his ever-loving wife, Helen: “You’re not protecting her [their daughter]. You’re protecting your pride.” She calls out in him what he is clinging to so desperately in the face of disappointment. Confronted by the loss of so many dreams and attachments, often good in and of themselves, pride presents itself as a false bulwark against the void that seems to loom in David’s life. This has become a common cry in popular culture: “Even if I lose everything, at least I have my dignity. I went out on my own terms.”

Aquinas teaches that pride is “the beginning of sin,” and in this movie, we see what happens when everything is stripped away and pride is backed into a tight corner. David lashes out in anger, and with his words, he wounds his family. Ultimately, however, pride is no true defense against loss and disappointment, and we see David eventually brought so low that he retreats to his bed, unable to help his family or even to get up. 

3. It is important to acknowledge to ourselves and confess to others our weaknesses and the areas where we feel unable to be a good man.

Aware of all his faults and failings, David is finally stirred by the love of his wife and the lyrics of a song written by his daughter: “You make everything, everything beautiful. You make everything, everything new.” He comes out of his dark room into the light of day, acknowledging his mistakes to his children and asking for their forgiveness. In gratitude, he takes a step of humility and action that leads toward the beautiful resolution of the film. 

The humility of confession shows itself as a true antidote to the bitter pill of pride. As this movie shows, swallowing your pride (that is, simply forcing it down) does not lead to true humility and freedom. Rather, it is by bringing our sins and weaknesses to the light that we allow our pride to be taken away and replaced by the peace of surrender. It is in receiving every gift and our very identity from God that we can hope to hear from our heavenly Father, “You’ll be a Man, my son!” (line 24).
